content.text: Good — the codebase already has an `osroot` package and a `readConfined` precedent. Two things genuinely change the shape of this work, so let me confirm before I start.

questions.question: There are 1402 `os.WriteFile` calls: 49 in production code, 46 in test harnesses (e2e/, integration_test/, testutil, benchutil, vogon), and 1307 in `_test.go` files. How far should this go?

options.label: Production only (49) + lint rule (Recommended)
options.description: Convert the 49 production sites, then add a forbidigo rule banning os.WriteFile. `.golangci.yaml` already exempts `_test.go` from forbidigo, so tests stay as-is by the project's own existing convention. Smallest diff, all of the actual security value.

options.label: Production + test harnesses (95)
options.description: Also convert e2e/, integration_test/, testutil, benchutil, vogon. These write into temp dirs so there's no traversal risk, but it makes the ban uniform for every non-`_test.go` file and lets the forbidigo rule apply without carve-outs.

options.label: Everything, all 1402
options.description: Also rewrite 1307 `_test.go` call sites. Tests write into t.TempDir(); this is pure churn with no security benefit and makes test setup noticeably more verbose, but leaves zero os.WriteFile in the tree.

questions.question: `os.Root` needs a root directory plus a relative path. Which anchor should the replacements use?

options.label: Parent dir, like readConfined (Recommended)
options.description: Add `osroot.WriteFileAt(path, data, perm)`: opens a root at filepath.Dir(path), writes filepath.Base(path). Drop-in one-line replacement at every site. Guarantees the final component can't be a symlink escape — the same guarantee settings.readConfined already provides for reads.

options.label: Real boundary, like openAllowedRoot
options.description: Anchor each write at a meaningful boundary (worktree root, git common dir, home, temp) and write a multi-segment relative path, so the whole path is confined, not just the last component. Stronger, but needs a per-site judgment call about which boundary applies and will reject writes outside them.

options.label: Parent dir now, boundary where one already exists
options.description: Use WriteFileAt as the default, but where the call site already holds a repo/common-dir/session root handle nearby, anchor there instead and write the longer relative path. Mixed, decided per site.

        if 'os.WriteFile(' in line and not is_comment:
            line = line.replace('os.WriteFile(', 'osroot.WriteFileAt(')
            n += line.count('osroot.WriteFileAt(')
        out_lines.append(line)
    if n == 0:

    src = '\n'.join(out_lines)

        # Insert into the last (project) group, keeping gofmt to sort it.
        newblock = block.rstrip('\n') + '\n\t' + IMPORT + '\n'
        src = src[:m.start(1)] + newblock + src[m.end(1):]

    changed.append((fp, n))

func TestWriteFileAt(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	dir := t.TempDir()
	path := filepath.Join(dir, "hello.txt")

	require.NoError(t, osroot.WriteFileAt(path, []byte("world"), 0o600))

	data, err := os.ReadFile(path) //nolint:gosec // test-controlled path
	require.NoError(t, err)
	assert.Equal(t, "world", string(data))
}

func TestWriteFileAt_Truncates(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	dir := t.TempDir()
	path := filepath.Join(dir, "hello.txt")

	require.NoError(t, osroot.WriteFileAt(path, []byte("a longer original"), 0o600))
	require.NoError(t, osroot.WriteFileAt(path, []byte("short"), 0o600))

	data, err := os.ReadFile(path) //nolint:gosec // test-controlled path
	require.NoError(t, err)
	assert.Equal(t, "short", string(data))
}

// WriteFileAt is a drop-in for os.WriteFile, so a missing parent directory must
// stay classifiable with os.IsNotExist. Returning the OpenRoot error wrapped
// would silently break callers that branch on it, since os.IsNotExist does not
// unwrap.
func TestWriteFileAt_MissingParentMatchesOSWriteFile(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	path := filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "nope", "f.txt")

	gotErr := osroot.WriteFileAt(path, []byte("x"), 0o600)
	wantErr := os.WriteFile(path, []byte("x"), 0o600) //nolint:forbidigo,gosec // parity baseline under test

	require.Error(t, gotErr)
	require.Error(t, wantErr)
	assert.Equal(t, os.IsNotExist(wantErr), os.IsNotExist(gotErr),
		"os.IsNotExist parity with os.WriteFile must hold")
	assert.ErrorIs(t, gotErr, os.ErrNotExist)
}

// The reason WriteFileAt exists: os.WriteFile would follow a symlinked final
// component and clobber the file it points at outside the directory.
func TestWriteFileAt_EscapingFinalComponentBlocked(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	dir := t.TempDir()
	outsideDir := t.TempDir()
	outside := filepath.Join(outsideDir, "secret.txt")
	require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(outside, []byte("original"), 0o600)) //nolint:forbidigo // fixture setup outside the root under test
	require.NoError(t, os.Symlink(outside, filepath.Join(dir, "innocent.txt")))

	err := osroot.WriteFileAt(filepath.Join(dir, "innocent.txt"), []byte("clobbered"), 0o600)
	require.Error(t, err, "write through an escaping symlink should be blocked")

	data, err := os.ReadFile(outside) //nolint:gosec // test-controlled path
	require.NoError(t, err)
	assert.Equal(t, "original", string(data), "file outside the root must be untouched")
}

// A symlink that stays inside the directory is legitimate and still followed,
// so confinement does not break in-root indirection.
func TestWriteFileAt_InRootSymlinkFollowed(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	dir := t.TempDir()
	target := filepath.Join(dir, "target.txt")
	require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(target, []byte("original"), 0o600)) //nolint:forbidigo // fixture setup
	require.NoError(t, os.Symlink("target.txt", filepath.Join(dir, "link.txt")))

	require.NoError(t, osroot.WriteFileAt(filepath.Join(dir, "link.txt"), []byte("updated"), 0o600))

	data, err := os.ReadFile(target) //nolint:gosec // test-controlled path
	require.NoError(t, err)
	assert.Equal(t, "updated", string(data))
}

changes what `main` is tested against, and the E2E leg goes red with no CLI commit
involved. Triage the agent version and the vendor account **before** bisecting our code.

(`npm view <pkg> time --json`). A vendor release landing inside the boundary window
beats any of our commits as a suspect. Confirm with the downloaded artifacts
(`gh run download <id> -n e2e-artifacts-<agent>`), which carry per-test `console.log`,
`git-log.txt`, and `entire-logs/` — diff a failing test's artifacts against the same
test from the last green run.

`TestCodexAppServerHooksList_BareWorktreeUsesLayoutRoot` (and its sibling at

to `/private/var`, so:

Done. All production `os.WriteFile` calls now go through `os.Root`.

**What changed** — 35 files, +204/−54:

- **New helper** `osroot.WriteFileAt(path, data, perm)` — opens an `os.Root` at `filepath.Dir(path)` and writes `filepath.Base(path)` through it. It's the write-side counterpart to the `settings.readConfined` pattern already in the codebase, and a true drop-in for `os.WriteFile`: same create/truncate semantics, same perm handling, errors returned unwrapped so `os.IsNotExist` still classifies a missing parent dir. I verified that parity rather than assuming it — returning the `OpenRoot` error wrapped would have silently broken those callers, since `os.IsNotExist` doesn't unwrap.
- **48 call sites** converted across 31 files. All of them take the plain form — the one file that already opens a root does so in a different function, so the "anchor at an existing root handle" case turned out to be empty.
- **15 stale `//nolint:gosec` directives** removed; gosec no longer sees these writes and `nolintlint` flagged every one.
- **forbidigo rule** banning `os.WriteFile`, plus `osroot` added to the agent-package import allowlist in `architecture_test.go` (it's stdlib-only, so it introduces no coupling — that guard test caught the omission).

**Verification:** lint 0 issues · 9988 unit tests pass · E2E canary 4/4 · integration 536 tests, 1 failure.

That one integration failure is **pre-existing, not from this change** — I proved it by running the same test in a throwaway worktree at clean `HEAD`, where it fails identically. `TestCodexAppServerHooksList_BareWorktreeUsesLayoutRoot` spawns the real `codex` binary, which resolves `/var` → `/private/var` on macOS while `t.TempDir()` doesn't. It skips when codex isn't installed, so it only bites developers running the local gate. I've noted it in memory; the fix is an `EvalSymlinks` on the expected path in the test, which I left alone as out of scope.

**One behavior change worth knowing about:** a final path component that is a symlink pointing *outside* its directory is now rejected instead of followed. That's the point of the change, but it's the same class of trap that CLAUDE.md records go-git hitting with `~/.config`. I checked the exposure and it's small — every agent hook-config write is repo-root relative (`.claude/`, `.cursor/`, `.factory/`…), git hooks resolve through `core.hooksPath` to a real directory, and a symlinked *parent* still works fine (`OpenRoot` resolves the root path itself). Where it can fire, the call sites return a wrapped error rather than swallowing it.

**Left out, per your scope call:** 46 sites in test harnesses (`e2e/`, `integration_test/`, `testutil`, `benchutil`, `vogon`) and 1307 in `_test.go`. Since those harnesses don't end in `_test.go`, the existing forbidigo exemption missed them and the new rule fired on all 43 lint-visible ones — so I added a carve-out scoped by message text rather than excluding forbidigo wholesale, which keeps the `os.Getwd` and go-git rules active in those files.

Establish os.Root anchors for the seven trees Entire reads and writes using names it does not control, including agent session IDs, tool-use IDs, investigation run IDs, git status output, and checkpoint tree entries fetched from a remote. Each tree has one owning abstraction, and operations beneath an anchor reject symlinks instead of merely relying on os.Root
  containment.

  ### Anchors

  One owning abstraction per tree: entiredir, gitdir, worktreedir, agent.SessionStore, agent.HookConfigFile, userdirs, and pluginRoot.

  Long-lived anchors are memoized through a single osroot.Shared registry. agent.SessionStore is intentionally opened per operation because transcript fallback search may probe hundreds of candidate directories; retaining those roots in the non-evicting registry would consume one file descriptor per candidate.

  Resolver-derived files must use the anchor for their owning tree. They must not create an anchor from filepath.Dir of the target being opened, because that places the caller-resolved components above the root and leaves them unenforced. Explicit caller-named settings and token-store paths are documented exceptions because the parent directory is itself part of the caller’s selection.

  TestRootBasesAreTrusted fails the build when a new root-opening site is not on the allowlist, or when an allowlisted site no longer opens a root.

  ### Refusals

  - .entire must be a real directory, and every direct entry must be a regular file or directory. Four distinct failure conditions are matched positively so the reported remedy fits the  fault.

  - Symlinks are refused, not followed or silently skipped, in trees Entire owns, including at a walk root and in every component beneath an anchor.

    fs.WalkDir obtains its root DirEntry using fs.Stat, which follows symlinks, while only entries below the root come from ReadDir. The previous callback guards inspected d.Type(), so
    they did not protect the walk root. A symlinked .entire/metadata/<session> could therefore be traversed and have its target committed and pushed. This protection had previously existed
    with filepath.Walk, which uses Lstat, and was lost during conversion.

  - Filesystem operations pin path components instead of checking and resolving them again. Parent directories are opened one component at a time, with symlinks rejected at every level.
    Reads, writes, directory creation, removal, enumeration, and walks then operate relative to those pinned descriptors. This closes the check/use gap where an attacker could replace a
    verified directory before the subsequent operation.

  - Worktree content read or modified by Entire also rejects symlink components where following them would redirect the operation. This includes agent hook configuration, managed agent
    scaffold files, .gitignore, .worktreeinclude, agent session files, and files read for trail-review selected text.

  - Settings resolved by Entire are never read through a link, enforced in the settings reader itself because eighteen call sites invoke settings.Load without passing through the pre-run
    guard. Explicit caller-selected settings paths trust the caller-selected parent as their root but still refuse a symlink at the target file.

  - “We could not find out” is not “there is nothing here.” WorktreeRoot falls back to the current directory only after Git positively reports that the directory is not in a repository. It
    does not fall back when Git is absent from $PATH, repository ownership is dubious, the context is cancelled, or repository discovery otherwise fails.

  ### Interrupted atomic writes

  jsonutil.WriteFileAtomicIn creates a temporary file named <base>.<16 hex>.tmp beside its target. Because .entire/metadata/<session> is copied wholesale into checkpoint trees, a hook
  killed during an atomic write could leave an orphan that was committed in every later checkpoint.

  ParseChunkIndex also previously used fmt.Sscanf("%03d"), which stops successfully at the first non-digit. A temporary file whose random suffix began with digits could therefore be
  interpreted as a transcript chunk.

  Checkpoint walks now recognize and ignore only the complete temporary-file naming pattern, while ParseChunkIndex accepts only an entirely numeric suffix.

  ### Repository opening
  gitrepo.OpenCurrent no longer falls back to OpenPath(".") when the worktree root cannot be established.

  The single caller that intentionally wants best-effort cwd behavior uses OpenCurrentOrCwd explicitly. It is dispatched from main.go after Cobra processing, reads only a policy ref, and
  discards every error.

Looked at it. **PR #2180 — "Confine Entire's filesystem use to `os.Root` anchors"** by Paulo Gomes: 183 files, +8,468/−2,641, open since 2026-08-30.

**It's the same idea I built for you on Thursday, done far more thoroughly — and it supersedes that work.** 31 of my 35 changed files are in its diff.

**What it does beyond what I did:**
- Defines **seven named anchors**, one owning abstraction per tree (`entiredir`, `gitdir`, `worktreedir`, `agent.SessionStore`, `agent.HookConfigFile`, `userdirs`, `pluginRoot`), memoized through an `osroot.Shared` registry.
- **Refuses symlinks outright** rather than merely confining them — `OpenNoFollow`, `ReadFileNoFollow`, `OpenFileNoFollow`, with parents pinned one component at a time and a `os.SameFile` re-check that closes the Lstat/Open race.
- Fixes a real vulnerability in passing: `fs.WalkDir` gets its root entry via `fs.Stat` (follows symlinks), so the existing callback guards never protected the *walk root* — a symlinked `.entire/metadata/<session>` could have its target committed and pushed. That protection existed under `filepath.Walk` (which uses `Lstat`) and was lost in conversion.
- Catches an orphan-temp-file bug: `ParseChunkIndex` used `fmt.Sscanf("%03d")`, which stops successfully at the first non-digit, so an interrupted atomic write's `.<hex>.tmp` could be read as a transcript chunk.

**The part you'll want to know about my work:** the PR body explicitly rules out the approach you picked. It says resolver-derived files *"must not create an anchor from `filepath.Dir` of the target being opened, because that places the caller-resolved components above the root and leaves them unenforced."* That is exactly what `osroot.WriteFileAt` does. It's the weaker of the two anchoring options I put to you, and this PR implements the stronger one properly. It also adds `TestRootBasesAreTrusted`, which fails the build for any root-opening site not on an allowlist — my helper wouldn't pass it.

So my recommendation is to **drop my 35-file change** rather than try to reconcile it.

**Two things in mine that the PR does *not* cover, worth salvaging:**
1. **No lint ban.** The PR adds no forbidigo rule, so `os.WriteFile` can drift back in. My `.golangci.yaml` rule (plus the harness carve-out) is a ~10-line standalone addition.
2. **Three production files it doesn't touch**, which still call `os.WriteFile` — `agent/pi/hooks.go:101`, `strategy/hooks.go:488` (the 0o755 git-hook writer), and `internal/coreapi/spec/normalize.go:89`.

**Current state: not close to merging.** No human review yet — only `cursor` and `copilot` bots commented; `reviewDecision` is `REVIEW_REQUIRED`. CI is red on `test`, `test-core`, `test-windows`, and Entire Gates. The `test-core` failure is direct fallout of one of its own design calls — `TestHandleLifecycleTurnEnd_EmptyRepository` expects a graceful no-op outside a git repo, and the PR deliberately removed `WorktreeRoot`'s cwd fallback, so it now errors instead.

content.text:
Answered by checking each one. **Yes for one, a qualified yes for a second, and no for the third** — so my earlier "strip it down to the lint rule plus those three files" was wrong on two of them.

**1. `internal/coreapi/spec/normalize.go` — yes, a real reason. Drop it.**
It's `//go:build ignore` + `package main`: a build-time codegen tool that never ships in the CLI. I just proved lint can't even see it — with `os.WriteFile` put back, forbidigo stayed silent, so the ban cannot enforce this file and any conversion here will silently drift back. It also means `go build ./...` never compiled my edit (it does compile — I checked separately — but nothing in CI would have told me otherwise). Both paths are compile-time constants, reading a committed spec and writing a committed generated artifact, no untrusted input anywhere. This is the PR's own "the parent directory is part of the caller's selection" exception in its purest form. Converting it is pure noise.

**2. `strategy/hooks.go:488` — a reason not to do it *this way*.**
The hooks dir comes from `git rev-parse --git-path hooks`, which honors `core.hooksPath` — that can be an absolute path anywhere on disk, or repo-relative outside `.git/`. So there's no owning anchor; it's neither `gitdir` nor `worktreedir` in general, and my `filepath.Dir` anchor buys nothing when the whole directory path is config-derived. The one genuine win — refusing a symlinked `post-commit`, which would otherwise write an **executable** through a link — needs the PR's `OpenFileNoFollow`. And that API *rejects `O_TRUNC`* while `writeHookFile` truncates, so a correct conversion means an atomic temp+rename that also preserves the 0o755 bit. That's design work, not a swap.

**3. `pi/hooks.go:101` — no good reason, and it looks like a gap in the PR.**
It writes `<worktree_root>/.pi/extensions/entire/index.ts`, structurally identical to the `.claude`/`.cursor`/`.codex`/`.factory` configs the PR routes through `agent.HookConfigFile`/`OpenHookConfig`. The PR body says "all built-in agents" and it *does* touch `pi/lifecycle.go` and `pi/pi.go` — but not `pi/hooks.go`. Worth raising on the PR; the fix belongs in `OpenHookConfig`, not in my helper.

The common thread: doing any of these with `WriteFileAt` adds the pattern the PR explicitly bans to files Paulo would then have to rework.

**Separately — a defect in my own branch that this turned up.** My "lint 0 issues" was from before I added `osroot_test.go`; I never re-linted after. Doing it now surfaced 7 redundant `//nolint:gosec` / `//nolint:forbidigo` directives in that test file (`_test.go` is already exempt from both). I've stripped them — lint is back to 0 issues and the osroot tests still pass.

So what's actually left worth keeping is just **the forbidigo rule**, which the PR has no equivalent of. My suggestion: drop the rest of my branch, and post the `pi/hooks.go` gap as a review comment on #2180. Want me to draft that comment? I won't post it without you asking.

Half right. The follow-up plan is sound, but the PR isn't mergeable as it stands.

**`mergeable: MERGEABLE` only means "no git conflicts with main."** GitHub's actual readiness field says `mergeStateStatus: BLOCKED`. Nothing has moved since yesterday — still on commit `1d863f6ed`, `REVIEW_REQUIRED`, no human review (only the `cursor` and `copilot` bots commented).

**And the red CI is real, not flakes — 8 genuine failures, all caused by the PR's own design changes:**

- **`test-windows`** — 7 failures, all in agent hook installation: `TestInstallHooks_WindowsWrapperProbe*`, `TestInstallHooks_WindowsProbe*`, `TestDiscoverAndRegister_RegistersBatOnWindows`. That's squarely the new `agent.HookConfigFile`/`OpenHookConfig` rework.
- **`test-core`** — `TestHandleLifecycleTurnEnd_EmptyRepository` expects a graceful no-op outside a git repo; the PR deliberately removed `WorktreeRoot`'s cwd fallback, so it now errors.
- **`test`** — not an independent failure; it's the aggregator gate (`[ "failure" = "success" ]` per upstream job) failing because of the two above.
- **`Entire Gates`** — also red.

So it needs Paulo to reconcile those tests with the new behavior before it can land.

**On the follow-up plan itself — yes, both belong after it, and there's a sequencing constraint worth knowing:**

The lint rule **cannot land before `pi/hooks.go` is fixed**. The PR doesn't touch that file, so `os.WriteFile` survives there; drop the forbidigo ban on top and lint goes red immediately. So it's either one follow-up doing both, or `pi/hooks.go` first and the rule second — not the reverse.

One caveat I can't fully verify: this worktree is a partial clone and `git grep` on the PR ref returned inconsistent results, so I can't confirm from here that `pi/hooks.go` is the *only* surviving `os.WriteFile` in non-test code on Paulo's branch. Worth a real check against the merged tree before adding the rule, or the ban may surface more sites than expected.

There's also an argument for letting the hook-config work settle before touching `pi/hooks.go` — it's the same family as the seven Windows failures, so it's the least stable part of the PR right now.

input.content:
---
name: os-root-concurrent-openat-enoent
description: "Go 1.26.6 os.Root returns spurious ENOENT on concurrent OpenFile under a just-created dir; plain os.* is immune. Breaks session-state flock in PR #2180"
metadata:
  type: reference
---

`os.Root` on **go1.26.6 darwin/arm64** returns spurious `ENOENT` from
`OpenFile` for a directory that provably exists, when several goroutines share
one `*os.Root`. `os.Root` documents itself as safe for concurrent use, so this
is a stdlib bug, not a misuse.

Stdlib-only reproduction (no repo deps): N goroutines each run
`root.Mkdir("d", 0o750)` tolerating `EEXIST`, then
`root.OpenFile("d/f", O_RDWR|O_CREATE, 0o600)`.

    os.Root       : mkdir-fail=0  open-ENOENT=52 / 200 goroutines
    plain os.*    : failures=0    / 200            <- control, immune

`mkdir-fail=0` is the important half: every goroutine's own `Mkdir` returned
nil or `EEXIST` **before** it called `OpenFile`, so the directory existed. Rate
is ~1-6 per 20 goroutines, so a single-digit concurrent fan-out reproduces it.

**Why it matters here (2026-08-31):** it is what makes
`TestRecordFilesTouched_ParallelMergesAreSerialized` fail ~60% of fresh
processes on cli PR #2180 ("Confine Entire's filesystem use to os.Root
anchors") while passing 20/20 on main. That PR routes filesystem work through
`os.Root` anchors, so `stateLockInCommonDir` does `MkdirAllNoSymlink(root,
"entire-session-locks")` then `flock.AcquireIn(root, ".../<id>.lock")` — the
open fails with `acquire state lock: open flock: openat
entire-session-locks/<id>.lock: no such file or directory`, the session-state
flock is never taken, and concurrent `FilesTouched` merges are **silently
lost** (20 goroutines → 15 or 19 files recorded, no error surfaced).

The PR's own `osroot.MkdirAllNoSymlink` is NOT at fault — it tolerates
`ErrExist` correctly, and an A/B probe shows plain `os.Root.Mkdir` failing at
the same rate.

**How to apply:** Do not "fix" this by patching `MkdirAllNoSymlink` or the
strategy test — neither is wrong. Any code path that shares one `*os.Root`
across goroutines and creates-then-opens needs either a retry on `ENOENT` or
serialization, until the stdlib is fixed. Confirm the Go version first: this
was found on go1.26.6, and it should be re-probed (and reported upstream)
before designing around it. The control above is the way to tell an `os.Root`
bug apart from a genuine missing directory. See
[[codex-integration-test-private-var]] for the other macOS-only trap in the
same PR's test suite.

content.text:
Mostly, yes — but I found something that should block the PR.

## Fixed (in a worktree, 5 files, +42/−8)

**1. `test-core` — `TestHandleLifecycleTurnEnd_EmptyRepository`**
The test hand-builds `.git/{objects,HEAD}` with no `refs/` — a shape real `git init` never produces, and which git rejects outright. On main that didn't matter because `OpenCurrent` fell back to `OpenPath(".")`; the PR removed that fallback, so `OpenRepository` now errors and the empty-repo guard never fires. A real `git init` works fine on the PR, so I replaced the fixture with `testutil.InitRepo` (the repo's own documented helper). The test now actually reaches the `"skipping checkpoint — will activate after first commit"` path it was written to pin, which it never did on the PR branch.

**2. `test-windows` — all 7 failures, one cause**
Every assertion passed; they died in `t.TempDir()` cleanup: *"The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process."* `OpenHookConfig` → `worktreedir.OpenAt` → `osroot.Shared` hands out a **process-wide, never-closed** root — on a temp dir. Invisible on Unix, fatal on Windows. Fixed with `t.Cleanup(osroot.ResetShared)` at the three setup sites (`t.Cleanup` is LIFO, so it runs before `RemoveAll` — I verified both that ordering and that `ResetShared` really closes the handle). Corroboration: the one Windows test in those packages that *didn't* fail is the one that never anchors a root.

**3. Bonus — a macOS-only failure CI can't see**
`TestOpenCurrent_RefusesToGuessWhenTheWorktreeRootIsUnresolvable` (new in this PR) compares `t.TempDir()` against git's answer: `/var/…` vs `/private/var/…`. Passes on Linux CI, fails on **every macOS dev machine**. Fixed with `EvalSymlinks`.

All four areas pass, lint is 0 issues, and `GOOS=windows go vet` is clean.

## Not fixed — and I don't think it should be

The full suite surfaced a fourth failure CI never reported: `TestRecordFilesTouched_ParallelMergesAreSerialized` fails **~60% of fresh single-iteration processes** on the PR, and **20/20 clean on main**. It's a silent lost update — 20 concurrent merges, 15 or 19 recorded, no error.

I chased it down to a **Go stdlib bug, not Paulo's code**. A 40-line dependency-free program reproduces it:

```
os.Root    : mkdir-fail=0   open-ENOENT=52 / 200 goroutines
plain os.*  : failures=0                    / 200   ← control, immune
```

`mkdir-fail=0` is the load-bearing half: every goroutine's own `Mkdir` returned nil or `EEXIST` *before* it called `OpenFile`, so the directory existed. `os.Root` documents itself as safe for concurrent use. An A/B probe clears `osroot.MkdirAllNoSymlink` specifically — plain `os.Root.Mkdir` fails at the same rate.

The consequence in this PR: `stateLockInCommonDir` creates the lock dir then opens the lock file through the same root, gets ENOENT, **the session-state flock is never taken**, and concurrent `FilesTouched` merges are silently lost. That's data loss in a concurrency-critical path, on go1.26.6.

I deliberately didn't paper over it. Patching the test or `MkdirAllNoSymlink` would hide a real defect, and designing the workaround (retry on ENOENT vs. serialize vs. pin the Go version) is Paulo's call. I've written it up in memory with the reproduction.

So: **the three CI-blocking failures are fixed, but I'd hold the PR on that fourth finding** rather than call it green.

My changes are uncommitted in a scratch worktree and I haven't touched Paulo's branch. Want me to push them to his branch, or post the `os.Root` finding as a review comment with the repro?

Let me correct my memory entry — my earlier characterization was wrong:

input.content:
---
name: os-root-concurrent-openat-enoent
description: "macOS-only Go bug: concurrent os.Root.OpenFile(same path, O_CREATE) returns spurious ENOENT. Present in 1.26.6/1.26.7/1.27.0. Breaks flock in cli PR #2180"
metadata:
  type: reference
---

On **darwin**, `os.Root.OpenFile` returns spurious `ENOENT` when several
goroutines `O_CREATE` the **same path** through one shared `*os.Root`.
`os.Root` documents itself as safe for concurrent use, so this is a stdlib bug.

**Trigger is narrow — get this right:** it is concurrent `O_CREATE` on *one
path*. Creating the parent concurrently is irrelevant, and so is nesting; a
flat single-component name fails just as hard. Measured 2026-08-31 with a
stdlib-only program, 50 trials x 20 goroutines = 1000 per cell:

| variant (all `os.Root` unless noted)      | 1.26.6 | 1.26.7 | 1.27.0 | linux/arm64 1.26.7 |
|-------------------------------------------|--------|--------|--------|--------------------|
| different file per goroutine              | 0      | 0      | 0      | 0 |
| different file + concurrent `Mkdir`       | 0      | 0      | 0      | 0 |
| **same file `d/f`**                       | **303**| **459**| **364**| **0** |
| **same file `f` (flat)**                  | **292**| **336**| **307**| **0** |
| same file, plain `os.*` (control)         | 0      | 0      | 0      | 0 |

So: **NOT fixed in 1.26.7 or 1.27.0**, and **Linux is immune** (arm64 verified;
amd64 not verified — it crashed under qemu emulation). Plain `os.*` is immune
everywhere, which is the control that tells an `os.Root` bug apart from a
genuinely missing directory.

**Why it matters (cli PR #2180, "Confine Entire's filesystem use to os.Root
anchors"):** flock is the worst case for this, because every caller opens the
*same* lock file with `O_RDWR|O_CREATE`. `stateLockInCommonDir` then fails with
`acquire state lock: open flock: openat entire-session-locks/<id>.lock: no such
file or directory`, the session-state flock is never taken, and concurrent
`FilesTouched` merges are **silently lost** (20 goroutines -> 15 or 19 files
recorded, no error). `TestRecordFilesTouched_ParallelMergesAreSerialized` fails
~60% of fresh processes on that branch and 0/20 on main. Because it is
macOS-only it does NOT show up in CI, so CI green does not clear it.

The PR's `osroot.MkdirAllNoSymlink` is **not** at fault — it tolerates
`ErrExist` correctly, and plain `os.Root.Mkdir` fails at the same rate.

**How to apply:** Don't patch `MkdirAllNoSymlink` or the strategy test; neither
is wrong. Any path where multiple goroutines/processes `O_CREATE` the same file
through a shared `*os.Root` needs a retry on `ENOENT`, or must create the file
once up front and then only open it without `O_CREATE`. Re-run the probe before
designing around it — mechanism is in the darwin `openat` path in
`os/root_unix.go` (`rootOpenFileNolog`, which always adds `O_NOFOLLOW`) via
`doInRoot` in `os/root_openat.go`; Linux takes the same code path but does not
reproduce, so the difference is below Go. See
[[codex-integration-test-private-var]] for the other macOS-only trap in the
same PR's suite.

content.text:
**No — not fixed in either.** And running this down changed two things I told you earlier.

| variant (all `os.Root` unless noted) | 1.26.6 | 1.26.7 | 1.27.0 | linux/arm64 1.26.7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| different file per goroutine | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| different file + concurrent `Mkdir` | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **same file `d/f`** | **303** | **459** | **364** | **0** |
| **same file `f` (flat)** | **292** | **336** | **307** | **0** |
| same file, plain `os.*` (control) | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

(50 trials × 20 goroutines = 1000 per cell, stdlib-only program.)

**Two corrections to what I said before:**

**1. The trigger is narrower than I described.** It has nothing to do with `Mkdir` or a just-created directory — those variants are clean. It's concurrent **`O_CREATE` on the same path**, and it fails just as hard on a flat single-component name. My earlier probe conflated the two because all 20 goroutines happened to open the same filename.

**2. It's macOS-only.** Linux is 0/1000 on every variant. That's why CI never saw it and why `test-core` reported only the lifecycle failure — **CI going green does not clear this**.

Both matter for the fix: "create the parent more carefully" wouldn't have helped, and anyone reproducing on a Linux box would conclude there's no bug.

**Why flock is the worst possible case for it:** every caller opens the *same* lock file with `O_RDWR|O_CREATE`. That's precisely the shape that fails. So on macOS the session-state flock silently isn't acquired and concurrent `FilesTouched` merges are lost with no error.

I also cleared Paulo's helper: `osroot.MkdirAllNoSymlink` tolerates `ErrExist` correctly, and plain `os.Root.Mkdir` fails at the same rate. The mechanism is in the darwin `openat` path (`rootOpenFileNolog` in `os/root_unix.go`, which always adds `O_NOFOLLOW`, via `doInRoot`) — Linux runs the same Go code and doesn't reproduce, so the divergence is below Go.

**Practical upshot for the PR:** since it's macOS-only, it isn't blocking his CI — my three fixes should get that green. But it is a real correctness bug for every macOS user of the CLI, not just a test annoyance. The workaround is either a retry on `ENOENT` around the lock open, or creating the lock file once up front and thereafter opening it without `O_CREATE`.

Two caveats: I couldn't verify linux/amd64 — the emulated run crashed in the Go runtime under qemu, so that's unverified rather than clean. And this looks worth an upstream Go issue; the 40-line reproduction is in the scratchpad at `osrootbug/` if you want to file it.

content.text:
**No open issue for this.** I searched all 7 `os.Root`-titled issues plus concurrent/race/darwin/ENOENT/O_CREATE/openat wordings and 2026-opened `os.Root` issues.

**Closest match — #75114 (closed, fixed):** *"`Root.MkdirAll` can return 'file exists' when called concurrently on the same path."* Different operation from mine (`MkdirAll`/EEXIST vs `OpenFile`/ENOENT — and my variant B shows `MkdirAll` isn't involved), but the **same shape**: a `Root` operation racing on one path and returning the wrong errno. It was fixed in CL 698215 and **backported to 1.24 and 1.25** within a day. That's the precedent to cite — the Go team already accepted this class as a real bug.

**Also relevant and open:** #73077 (use `openat2`+`RESOLVE_BENEATH` on Linux) and #73079 (use `O_NOFOLLOW_ANY` on macOS). #73077 still being open is exactly why Linux runs the same component-wise Go code yet is immune.

**While searching I also nailed the mechanism — and it's below Go**, which corrects the `O_NOFOLLOW` guess I floated earlier:

| call (darwin/arm64, 1000 goroutines each) | failures |
|---|---|
| `os.OpenFile(fullpath, O_CREAT)` | 0/1000 |
| `os.OpenFile(fullpath, O_CREAT\|O_NOFOLLOW)` | 0/1000 |
| **`unix.Openat(dirfd, "f", O_CREAT)`** | **336/1000** |
| **`unix.Openat(dirfd, "f", O_CREAT\|O_NOFOLLOW)`** | **299/1000** |

`O_NOFOLLOW` is not the trigger. Plain **`openat` + `O_CREAT` racing on one name returns spurious ENOENT on darwin**, with no Go `os.Root` in the picture, while full-path `open(2)` is atomic. `os.Root` is built entirely on `openat`, which is exactly why it inherits this and plain `os.*` doesn't — and why it's macOS-only, same-path-only, and unaffected by `Mkdir`.

So strictly the defect is xnu/APFS, not Go's logic. It's still worth filing against Go: `O_CREAT` is meant to be atomic, `os.Root` is the only reason ordinary Go code hits it, and #75114 shows they'll take a retry-style fix.

## The process

It's **two reports, and neither uses the repo code.**

**1. golang/go — the one worth filing.** Go isn't at fault, but `os.Root` is how ordinary Go code hits this, and Go already normalizes OS quirks in the exact function involved:

```go
// AIX returns ELOOP instead of EEXIST for a dangling symlink.
// Convert this to EEXIST so it matches ErrExists.
```

So "retry `ENOENT` when `O_CREAT` is set on darwin" fits existing practice rather than asking for something new.

Mechanics: run `go bug`, which opens a pre-filled GitHub issue with your `go env`. Fill in what you did / expected / saw. No proposal process — it's a bug. Title in their convention: `os: Root.OpenFile returns spurious ENOENT for concurrent O_CREATE on the same path on macOS`. The body should carry the Go repro, the C repro (proves it's below Go, which preempts the first triage question), the version matrix (1.26.6 / 1.26.7 / 1.27.0 all affected), and the platform matrix (Linux clean). Cite **#75114** as precedent — same class, fixed and backported in a day. Worth noting the retry can't be unbounded; that exact concern was raised on #75114.

**2. Apple — the actual defect.** Feedback Assistant, macOS → Kernel. Attach `repro.c`. Realistically a black hole, but it's where the bug lives, and the Go issue is stronger if it can say the kernel side was reported.

**What not to do:** don't file with Entire's code or the `TestRecordFilesTouched` failure. That's the symptom, and it'd get closed as unreproducible.

Two caveats to state honestly in the issue: I only tested **arm64** (Intel Macs unverified — the Linux/amd64 leg crashed under qemu), and only **macOS 26.6 / 25G72**. A second machine or an older macOS would strengthen it, and triage will likely ask.

Separately: **don't let Entire wait on either.** Whatever Go does won't land in a release you can depend on soon, so the CLI needs its own fix — retry on `ENOENT`, or create the lock file once and thereafter open it without `O_CREATE`.

content.text:
Short answer: **no, not a vulnerability — but it has one security-adjacent property worth naming.**

**It doesn't weaken `os.Root`'s guarantee.** The failure is a spurious *failure*, never a spurious success. It never opens the wrong file, never escapes the root, never follows a symlink it shouldn't. `os.Root` exists as a traversal/TOCTOU boundary, and this bug leaves that boundary intact — which means the PR's entire security thesis still holds. My blast-radius data backs that: `O_EXCL` behaves perfectly (950 correct EEXIST, zero spurious ENOENT), so atomic create-exclusive semantics are never subverted.

**The security-adjacent part:** the manufactured errno is `ENOENT`, which *means* "does not exist". That's exactly the error fail-open code keys on — `if os.IsNotExist(err) { /* no policy file, skip the check */ }`. So the audit question for any codebase adopting `os.Root` is: *do we skip a security check when a file appears absent?*

**For Entire I checked that, and the answer is no.** The split falls out cleanly along `O_CREATE`:

- **Security-relevant reads are unaffected.** Redaction scanner selection, OPF command trust, and the local-settings-layer rejection all load through `readConfined` → `ReadFileNoFollow` → `root.Open` with **no `O_CREATE`**. Per the table, pure reads are 0/1000.
- **`O_EXCL` sites are unaffected** — `jsonutil/write.go`'s atomic temp file, the session `.agent`/`.banner` sentinels, opencode's stage export.
- **Affected sites are all integrity/availability, not confidentiality or privilege:** the session-state flock (lost `FilesTouched` merges), `pushqueue.go` (a checkpoint ref might not get queued), `logging/logger.go` (first-run log file creation).

And OPF's pre-push path is fail-*closed* on error, so a failure there blocks the push rather than shipping under-redacted content — the safe direction.

**Exploitability is essentially nil.** You'd need local code execution already, racing concurrent creation of a not-yet-existent file, and the payoff is corrupted session metadata. It's a first-creation-only race, so in a real repo the lock file exists after the first run and the window closes. Not a remote or privilege-escalation primitive.

So I'd call it **integrity/reliability, not security** — and concretely: file the Go issue through the **normal public tracker, not security@golang.org**. Routing it as a security report would be wrong and would just add triage noise.

One honest caveat: I verified the main config-loading paths, not every `IsNotExist` branch in the codebase. If you want certainty, the targeted audit is "every `errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist)` on a root-based open that gates a check" — that's a bounded grep I can run.

Correcting my first read on the CGO question — repeated runs show it's noise:

```
CGO=0:  441, 484, 512  / 1000
CGO=1:  467, 453, 455  / 1000
```

**No difference.** The 61/172 in that first comparison was cold-run variance, not a CGO effect. Which is what the pure-C repro already implied: `CGO_ENABLED` doesn't change which syscall xnu executes, and on darwin Go routes through libSystem either way. So there's no "turn off cgo" escape hatch.

## On exploit leverage: no, and here's the specific reason

The probe was designed to find leverage, and every channel came back clean:

- **No wrong-object access.** All 1,194 successful opens across 200 trials saw the *same* inode with mode 0600. No inode confusion, no type confusion, no cross-file access. That absence is decisive — it's exactly what a TOCTOU/symlink primitive would need.
- **No lost create.** Zero trials ended with the file missing. You can't use this to make a privileged process fail to create a sentinel and then slot your own in.
- **No permission corruption.** Zero files with an unexpected mode.
- **`O_EXCL` is completely unaffected** — 950 correct `EEXIST`, zero spurious `ENOENT`. This is the one that matters most: `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` *is* the security-critical idiom (lockfiles, PID files, temp files), and it's intact.

The strongest thing an attacker gets is: race a victim's `O_CREAT` so the victim receives `ENOENT` instead of a handle. But they can't substitute a file — the file that lands is the winner's, correctly moded — and they already need local concurrent execution. Winning a create race against a non-`O_EXCL` open is a pre-existing hazard that exists with or without this bug; that's *why* `O_EXCL` exists. So it adds no new primitive.

Net: it's a **bug amplifier, not a primitive**. Its only security-adjacent property is that it forges the specific errno (`ENOENT` = "does not exist") that fail-open code branches on. That makes it dangerous only in combination with a caller that skips a check on "file absent" — which is a caller bug.

**Where I'd look next if you want to be thorough**, since I only tested regular files, same-name contention, one directory, APFS, as a single uid:
- whether the same race hits `mkdirat`, `symlinkat`, `linkat`, `renameat` — if `renameat` or `linkat` can be made to fail or misbehave, that's a much more interesting story than `openat`
- a world-writable sticky directory (`/tmp`) with a cross-uid racer, which is the classic setting where create races turn security-relevant

Those are cheap to test if you want them before filing — it'd also make the report stronger. But on what's measured so far, this is a correctness bug, not a vulnerability, and it should go to the public tracker rather than a security channel.

Racing one name, 20 threads × 200 trials:

```
mkdirat      ok=200  EEXIST=3800  ENOENT=0
symlinkat    ok=200  EEXIST=3800  ENOENT=0
linkat       ok=200  EEXIST=3800  ENOENT=0
renameat     ok=4000 (all correct)

The one broken case is the only operation with a **create-or-open fallback** — create fails `EEXIST`, retry as open. So the racy retry is the prime suspect, not path resolution. That's a much stronger lead for the issue than "os.Root is flaky", and it's the kind of narrowing that gets a kernel bug triaged instead of closed.

content.text:
Exactly right on both counts, and the second half is the important one.

**`CGO_ENABLED=0` genuinely disables cgo** — no C compiler, no FFI. But on **darwin that doesn't mean "no libc."** Both binaries link the same thing:

```
CGO_ENABLED=1  →  /usr/lib/libSystem.B.dylib, /usr/lib/libresolv.9.dylib
CGO_ENABLED=0  →  /usr/lib/libSystem.B.dylib, /usr/lib/libresolv.9.dylib   ← identical
```

And the pure-Go binary still carries libSystem trampolines:

```
_syscall.libc_open_trampoline.abi0
_syscall.libc_stat_trampoline.abi0
```

That's the piece worth naming: Apple doesn't guarantee a stable raw syscall ABI — only libSystem is supported — so Go's darwin runtime *always* routes syscalls through it via `//go:cgo_import_dynamic` trampolines. Those directives share cgo's name but aren't cgo; they're dynamic-linking machinery the runtime uses unconditionally. This is also why you can't produce a static Go binary on macOS the way you can on Linux, where Go really does issue raw `SYSCALL` instructions and `CGO_ENABLED=0` gets you a fully static binary.

**But your second sentence is the one that actually settles it.** Even if Go *did* bypass libSystem, it wouldn't matter, because the layer below is common to everything:

```
Go (cgo on or off) ─┐
                    ├─→ libSystem openat() → kernel trap → xnu VFS  ← bug lives here
C (repro.c) ────────┘
```

`repro.c` is compiled C with no Go anywhere and reproduces at 631–768/1000. libSystem's `openat` is a thin trap wrapper. So no toolchain flag, language, or runtime can route around it — which is exactly why the measurements came out flat at ~450/1000 either way, and why "just disable cgo" was never going to be a workaround.

The practical upshot for the write-up: the C repro is what makes the report land, because it preempts the first triage response ("this is a Go runtime issue"). The `CGO_ENABLED` matrix is a useful supporting line — it shows the reporter already ruled out the toolchain.

Handoff: a macOS kernel race in openat(O_CREAT) that we found via Go's os.Root — your job is a test repo + GitHub Actions macOS-runner matrix, incl. whether older macOS is affected. You have no context from the originating session, so everything you need is below. Reproductions are staged at /tmp/claude-501/macos-openat-bug/ (c/ and go/), already verified runnable.

THE BUG
On darwin, `openat(dirfd, name, O_CREAT)` WITHOUT O_EXCL, when several threads race on the same not-yet-existing name, returns spurious ENOENT to most callers. The winner creates the file correctly; the losers get ENOENT instead of a handle to the just-created file. Reproduces in pure C with no Go involved.

WHAT IS AND ISN'T AFFECTED (all measured, 20 threads x 200 trials each)
- openat + O_CREAT (no O_EXCL), file absent  -> BROKEN, ~25-75% spurious ENOENT
- openat + O_CREAT|O_EXCL                    -> correct (one winner, rest EEXIST, zero ENOENT)
- openat + O_CREAT, file already exists      -> clean
- openat O_RDONLY / O_RDWR on existing file  -> clean (reads unaffected)
- open(fullpath, O_CREAT)                    -> clean (this is the key control)
- mkdirat / symlinkat / linkat / renameat    -> all clean, zero ENOENT
- Linux (arm64, go1.26.7 in docker)          -> clean, 0/1000
So it is unique to the one operation with a create-or-open fallback (create fails EEXIST -> retry as open). That racy retry is the prime suspect, not path resolution. This is the strongest lead in the report — please don't lose it.

NOT A SECURITY VULN — verified, don't re-litigate unless you find new evidence
Strictly fail-closed: zero trials with no winner, zero trials where the file was missing afterwards, zero inode confusion (all successful openers saw the same inode), zero permission corruption. With the raced name a dangling symlink pointing outside the dir (classic /tmp attack shape) the symlink was never clobbered into a regular file and no opener ever got a non-target inode. Same in a world-writable sticky (01777) dir. It only forges the errno ENOENT ("does not exist"), so it is a bug amplifier for fail-open callers, never a primitive. => public tracker, NOT security@golang.org.

DATA POINTS SO FAR (both Apple Silicon)
- macOS 26.6  / build 25G72 / M4 Max : 2638 spurious ENOENT / 4000
- macOS 26.6.2/ build 25G83 / M5     : 1544 / 4000
Rate swings a lot with scheduling (I've seen 966-3034 on one machine). Only the two control rows make a run interpretable — always report them.

YOUR TASKS
1. Test repo. Small, standalone, public-ready — it will be linked from a golang/go issue, so no Entire code in it. Suggest: the C probe (definitive, proves it's below Go) + the Go/os.Root probe (shows why Go users hit it) + a README with the results matrix.
2. GitHub Actions macOS runner matrix. Check current runner labels first (image lineup moves; today is 2026-08-31). Historically macos-13 = Intel/x86_64, macos-14+ = arm64.
   *** x86_64 is the highest-value missing data point *** and not just for coverage: arm64 has a weaker memory model than x86 TSO, so a missing barrier in the kernel would surface on Apple Silicon and could be genuinely invisible on Intel. Either outcome improves the report — reproduces => arch-independent logic bug; clean on Intel => strong hint it's memory-ordering, which is a much sharper lead.
3. Older macOS. Use the older runner images to find whether this predates the current release, and ideally bisect roughly when it appeared. "Regression in 26.x" vs "always been there" changes the framing a lot.

RUNNING IT
/tmp/claude-501/macos-openat-bug/c/portable-check.sh is self-contained (needs only cc, writes to a temp dir it cleans up) and prints a VERDICT line: REPRODUCES / does NOT reproduce / ANOMALOUS. ANOMALOUS means the controls also failed => harness or environment at fault, not the kernel; investigate before reporting. Note CI runners are often 2-4 cores, so the rate may be lower than a laptop; if you get 0, raise thread count and trials before concluding "clean", and say what you tried.

CONTEXT FOR THE EVENTUAL ISSUE (don't file anything without the user's explicit approval)
- Go is affected because os.Root is built entirely on openat; plain os.* uses full-path open and is immune. Affected in go1.26.6, 1.26.7 and 1.27.0 (not fixed).
- CGO_ENABLED makes no difference (441/484/512 vs 467/453/455 per 1000) — darwin always routes syscalls through libSystem, cgo or not. No build-flag workaround exists.
- No existing golang/go issue. Closest precedent to cite: #75114 "Root.MkdirAll can return 'file exists' when called concurrently on the same path" — same class, different op, fixed in CL 698215 and backported to 1.24/1.25 within a day. Also open/related: #73077 (openat2+RESOLVE_BENEATH on Linux, still open — why Linux runs the same Go code yet is immune) and #73079 (O_NOFOLLOW_ANY on macOS).
- Two reports are in scope eventually: golang/go (ask them to retry ENOENT when O_CREAT is set; note the retry can't be unbounded, that concern was raised on #75114) and Apple Feedback Assistant (macOS -> Kernel) for the actual defect.
